metadata.title: Java MCQ Quiz
metadata.description: 100 multiple-choice questions covering Core Java, OOP, Collections, Multithreading, Exceptions, and Java 8+ features. Derived one-to-one from the Java Learn question bank, so every quiz item reinforces a concept you can go back and read.

questions.question: What is Java?
options: A compiled, platform-dependent language like C++
A high-level, OOP, platform-independent language developed by James Gosling
A scripting language that runs only in browsers
A database query language used with Oracle
questions.explanation: Java is high-level, OOP, and platform-independent. Its bytecode + JVM enables 'write once, run anywhere'.

questions.question: Why is Java platform-independent?
options: It compiles directly to native machine code for each OS
The javac compiler produces bytecode that any JVM can execute
It uses C++ headers to ensure cross-platform compatibility
It relies on the operating system kernel for portability
questions.explanation: javac produces bytecode (.class), not machine code. Any machine with a compatible JVM runs the same bytecode.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes JDK, JRE, and JVM?
options: JVM = JDK + JRE + tools
JRE = JVM + tools; JDK = JRE + standard libraries
JVM runs bytecode; JRE = JVM + libraries; JDK = JRE + compiler + tools
JDK and JRE are the same; JVM is a subset of JDK
questions.explanation: JVM runs bytecode. JRE = JVM + standard libraries (enough to run). JDK = JRE + javac + tools (needed to develop).

questions.question: Is Java a purely object-oriented language?
options: Yes, everything in Java is an object
Yes, because it supports all four OOP pillars
No, because it has primitive types (int, char, boolean, etc.) that are not objects
No, because it doesn't support multiple inheritance
questions.explanation: Java has 8 primitive types that are not objects. A purely OO language treats everything as an object.

questions.question: What is bytecode in Java?
options: Machine code specific to a particular processor
An intermediate, platform-neutral instruction set produced by the Java compiler
The source code written by the developer
Binary code stored directly in RAM
questions.explanation: Bytecode is an intermediate instruction set. The JVM either interprets it or JIT-compiles it to native code at runtime.

questions.question: What does the JIT compiler do?
options: Compiles Java source code to bytecode before execution
Validates bytecode for security vulnerabilities
Compiles frequently executed bytecode to native machine code at runtime
Links class files together at compile time
questions.explanation: Just-In-Time compiler compiles 'hot spots' (frequently run bytecode) into native code at runtime for better performance.

questions.question: What is the role of a ClassLoader in Java?
options: Compiles .java files to .class files
Loads class files into JVM memory on demand following parent-delegation
Manages garbage collection of unused classes
Provides JIT compilation for hot methods
questions.explanation: ClassLoader loads class files into memory on demand. Hierarchy: Bootstrap → Extension → Application loaders with parent-delegation.

questions.question: Which memory areas are managed by the JVM?
options: Only the Heap and Stack
Heap, Stack, and CPU cache
Heap, Stack, Method Area/Metaspace, PC Register, Native Method Stack
Code Segment, Data Segment, and BSS Segment
questions.explanation: JVM manages: Heap (objects), Stack (frames), Method Area/Metaspace (class metadata), PC Register, Native Method Stack.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes Stack vs Heap memory in the JVM?
options: Stack is thread-local and holds method frames and local variables; Heap is shared and holds all objects and arrays
Heap is thread-local and holds method frames; Stack is shared and holds objects
Both Stack and Heap are thread-local and are garbage collected identically
Stack stores objects; Heap stores only static variables
questions.explanation: Stack is thread-local, fast, and holds method calls plus local primitives/references. Heap is shared across threads, holds all objects, and is managed by the GC.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals()?
options: == compares content; .equals() compares references
Both compare content identically for every class
== works only on primitives; .equals() works only on Strings
== compares references (same object in memory); .equals() compares content as defined by the class
questions.explanation: == is reference comparison. .equals() is value comparison — String and wrapper classes override it; Object.equals() defaults to == behaviour.

questions.question: Which set best describes the main features of Java?
options: Simple, object-oriented, platform-independent, secure, robust, multithreaded, portable, high-performance
Pointer arithmetic, manual memory management, and operator overloading
Multiple class inheritance, destructors, and header files
Compiled-only execution with no runtime environment
questions.explanation: Java is simple, OOP, platform-independent, secure, robust, architecture-neutral, portable, multithreaded, distributed, dynamic, and high-performance via JIT.

questions.question: What is the default value of a local variable in Java?
options: 0 for numeric types and null for references
null for all types regardless of declaration
There is none — local variables must be explicitly initialized before use
false for all types until assigned
questions.explanation: Local variables have no default and the compiler enforces initialization. Only instance and class variables get defaults (0, false, null).

questions.question: Can a Java program execute without a main() method?
options: Yes, a static block can fully replace main() in any Java version
No — since Java 7 the JVM strictly requires main() as the entry point
Yes, the constructor runs automatically instead
Yes, if the class implements Runnable
questions.explanation: Historically a static block could print output before main ran, but the JVM still required main. Since Java 7 it is strictly required.

questions.question: What is the difference between final, finally, and finalize()?
options: All three are keywords used exclusively for exception handling
final closes resources, finally makes a variable constant, finalize() starts the GC
final and finalize() are identical; finally is a loop construct
final is a keyword for constants/non-overridable members, finally is a block that always runs, finalize() was a GC callback deprecated since Java 9
questions.explanation: final = constant variable / non-overridable method / non-extendable class. finally = cleanup block after try/catch. finalize() = old GC hook, deprecated since Java 9.

questions.question: What is a package in Java?
options: A namespace that groups related classes and interfaces, avoiding name clashes and providing access control
A compiled archive of .class files that the JVM executes directly
A special class that contains only static methods
A memory region where all class metadata is stored
questions.explanation: Packages group related types into a namespace. Benefits: no name collisions, access control, and easier code organization.

questions.question: What are the four pillars of OOP?
options: Abstraction, Aggregation, Composition, Association
Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, Abstraction
Classes, Objects, Methods, Constructors
Overloading, Overriding, Hiding, Shadowing
questions.explanation: The four pillars are Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction.

questions.question: What is encapsulation?
options: Exposing all fields as public so any class can modify them
Deriving a new class from an existing one
Bundling data and behaviour in a class and restricting direct field access via private fields with public getters/setters
Allowing one method name to have multiple implementations
questions.explanation: Encapsulation bundles fields and methods together and hides internal state behind private fields exposed through getters/setters.

questions.question: What is inheritance in Java?
options: A mechanism where a subclass acquires the fields and methods of a superclass using the extends keyword
A mechanism for hiding implementation details behind an interface
The ability of a method to accept different parameter lists
A way to prevent a class from being extended
questions.explanation: A subclass inherits from a superclass via extends. Java allows single inheritance for classes and multiple inheritance via interfaces.

questions.question: Why doesn't Java support multiple inheritance with classes?
options: Because the JVM cannot load more than one class at a time
To avoid the diamond problem — ambiguity when two parents define the same method
Because extends and implements are the same keyword internally
Because it would break garbage collection
questions.explanation: The diamond problem creates ambiguity. Java solves it by allowing one superclass but multiple implemented interfaces.

questions.question: What is polymorphism?
options: The ability to hide fields behind getters and setters
The ability of a class to inherit from multiple parents
The process of converting an object into a byte stream
'One interface, many implementations' — compile-time via overloading and runtime via overriding
questions.explanation: Polymorphism means one interface with many implementations. Compile-time = method overloading; runtime = method overriding.

questions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and overriding?
options: Overloading: same name, different parameters, same class, resolved at compile time. Overriding: subclass redefines a parent method with the same signature, resolved at runtime
Overloading happens at runtime; overriding happens at compile time
Overloading requires inheritance; overriding requires the same class
Both require a different return type and identical parameters
questions.explanation: Overloading is compile-time (static) polymorphism; overriding is runtime (dynamic) polymorphism resolved via dynamic dispatch.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts an abstract class with an interface?
options: An abstract class allows multiple inheritance; an interface allows only single inheritance
An interface can have constructors and instance fields; an abstract class cannot
An abstract class can have constructors, fields and concrete methods with single inheritance; an interface allows multiple inheritance and, since Java 8, default and static methods
They became completely identical in Java 8
questions.explanation: Abstract class: abstract + concrete methods, fields, constructors, single inheritance. Interface: multiple inheritance, plus default/static methods since Java 8 and private methods since Java 9.

questions.question: Can a class be declared private or protected in Java?
options: Yes, any class can be declared private or protected
A top-level class can only be public or package-private; nested classes can be private or protected
No class in Java can ever be private
Only interfaces can be declared protected
questions.explanation: Top-level classes are limited to public or package-private (no modifier). Inner/nested classes may be private or protected.

questions.question: What is a constructor in Java?
options: A special block with the same name as the class that runs on object creation to initialize state; the compiler supplies a no-arg default if none is defined
A static method that returns a new instance of the class
A method called just before the object is garbage collected
A block that runs once when the class is first loaded into memory
questions.explanation: A constructor shares the class name and initializes the object's state at creation. If you define none, the compiler adds a default no-arg constructor.

questions.question: What is the difference between default, parameterized, and copy constructors?
options: Java automatically provides all three for every class
A copy constructor is generated by the compiler whenever clone() is called
A parameterized constructor cannot coexist with a default one
Default takes no args and is compiler-supplied if none is defined; parameterized takes args to initialize fields; copy takes another instance to duplicate state and must be written manually
questions.explanation: Unlike C++, Java does not generate a copy constructor — you write it yourself. Defining any constructor removes the compiler's default one.

questions.question: Can a constructor be final, static, or abstract?
options: Yes, all three modifiers are allowed on constructors
No — constructors aren't inherited (so final is meaningless), they act on instances (so static is wrong), and they need a body (so abstract is wrong)
Only static is allowed, for singleton classes
Only final is allowed, to prevent subclass construction
questions.explanation: None of the three is legal on a constructor, and each for a different reason worth being able to state.

questions.question: What does the this keyword refer to?
options: A reference to the parent class object
A keyword that makes a variable a class-level constant
A reference to the current object — used for instance fields, to chain constructors via this(...), or to pass the current object
A keyword usable only inside static methods
questions.explanation: this refers to the current instance. It disambiguates shadowed fields, chains constructors, and passes the current object to other methods.

questions.question: What does the super keyword do?
options: References the immediate parent class — to call parent methods, access parent fields, or invoke the parent constructor via super(...)
References the topmost Object class in every hierarchy
Marks a method as non-overridable
Grants access to all private members of the parent class
questions.explanation: super refers to the immediate parent. super.method(), super.field, and super(...) for the parent constructor.

questions.question: What does the static keyword mean?
options: It makes a member immutable so its value can never change
It marks a field, method, block or nested class as belonging to the class itself rather than to instances, shared across all objects
It prevents a class from ever being instantiated
It forces the JVM to keep the object in the heap permanently
questions.explanation: Static members belong to the class, are shared by all instances, and are loaded once when the class is loaded.

questions.question: Can you override a static method in Java?
options: Yes, exactly like instance methods
Yes, but only if the subclass is in the same package
Yes, but only if the method is also final
No — static methods belong to the class, so a subclass hides them rather than overriding them, and polymorphism does not apply
questions.explanation: This is method hiding, not overriding. Because static binding is used, the reference type decides which method runs.

questions.question: Why are Strings immutable in Java?
options: Because the JVM cannot allocate mutable objects on the heap
Because String is a primitive type in Java
For security, thread safety and String Pool sharing — and it also lets the hash code be cached
So that StringBuilder can extend String
questions.explanation: Immutability makes Strings safe for passwords/class loaders/URLs, inherently thread-safe, poolable, and lets hashCode be cached.

questions.question: What is the String Pool?
options: A special region of the heap where String literals are stored so identical literals share one object
A thread pool used to process String operations in parallel
A cache in the Method Area holding compiled regular expressions
A stack region where all String references are stored
questions.explanation: Writing String s = "hello" twice makes both references point to the same pooled object, saving memory.

questions.question: What is the difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer?
options: All three are immutable and differ only in performance
String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and not thread-safe (fastest); StringBuffer is mutable and synchronized (thread-safe, slower)
StringBuilder is thread-safe while StringBuffer is not
StringBuffer and StringBuilder are immutable; String is mutable
questions.explanation: Prefer StringBuilder in single-threaded code. StringBuffer's synchronization costs performance and is rarely needed.

questions.question: What is the difference between String s = "abc" and String s = new String("abc")?
options: Both always create exactly one object in the String Pool
The literal form creates a new heap object each time; new String() reuses the pool
The literal reuses the String Pool (one object); new String() forces a separate heap object in addition to the pool entry
There is no difference — the compiler rewrites both identically
questions.explanation: The literal form is pooled and shared. new String() always allocates a distinct heap object, so potentially two objects exist.

questions.question: How should you compare two Strings in Java?
options: Use equals() for content, equalsIgnoreCase() for case-insensitive, compareTo() for lexicographic order — never == unless you want reference equality
Always use == because Java interns every String
Use compareTo() only, since equals() is not defined for String
Use the matches() method for all comparisons
questions.explanation: == compares references and only appears to work for pooled literals — which is exactly what makes it a dangerous habit.

questions.question: What does the intern() method do?
options: Converts a String into a StringBuilder
Permanently removes the String from the heap
Compares two Strings and returns a boolean
Returns the canonical pooled representation, adding the String to the pool first if it isn't already there
questions.explanation: intern() returns the pooled reference for a String, adding it to the pool if absent — useful for making == work on runtime-built strings.

questions.question: Is String a primitive or an object in Java?
options: A primitive type, like int and char
An object — java.lang.String; Java has no primitive string type
A primitive that is autoboxed into an object when needed
Neither — it is a compiler-level construct with no runtime type
questions.explanation: String is a class in java.lang. Java's 8 primitives are byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean — String is not among them.

questions.question: Can you use a String in a switch statement?
options: Yes, since Java 7; before that switch only supported primitives and enums
No, switch never supports String
Yes, but only if the String is interned manually first
Yes, since Java 5 along with enums
questions.explanation: String support in switch arrived in Java 7. Internally the compiler switches on hashCode and then confirms with equals().

questions.question: What is the output of "10" + 20 + 30?
options: The String '102030'
A compile-time error
questions.explanation: Evaluation is left-to-right: "10"+20 becomes "1020" (String concatenation), then "1020"+30 becomes "102030".

questions.question: What is the simplest way to reverse a String in Java?
options: Call the built-in String.reverse() method
Use new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString(), or iterate from the end manually
Call Collections.reverse(s) directly on the String
Strings cannot be reversed because they are immutable
questions.explanation: String has no reverse() method. StringBuilder.reverse() is the standard approach; manual iteration is the common coding-round variant.

questions.question: What is the Java Collections Framework?
options: A unified architecture for storing and manipulating groups of objects, with core interfaces Collection, List, Set, Queue and Map
A package of utility classes for file and network I/O
A set of primitive array helpers built into the language
A concurrency library introduced in Java 8
questions.explanation: The framework unifies group-of-object handling. Note that Map is a core interface but deliberately does not extend Collection.

questions.question: Why doesn't Map extend Collection?
options: Because Map was added to Java much later than Collection
Because a Map cannot be iterated over
Because a Map stores key-value pairs, so the Collection contract (add(E), remove(E)) does not fit naturally
Because Map is an abstract class rather than an interface
questions.explanation: The single-element Collection contract cannot express key-value semantics, so Map was kept as a separate root interface by design.

questions.question: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
options: ArrayList gives O(1) insertion anywhere; LinkedList gives O(1) random access
ArrayList is a dynamic array with O(1) random access but slower mid-list insertions; LinkedList is a doubly-linked list with O(1) head/tail insertion but O(n) random access
Both are backed by arrays and differ only in thread safety
LinkedList uses less memory per element than ArrayList
questions.explanation: ArrayList wins on indexed access; LinkedList wins on head/tail modification but pays extra memory per node.

questions.question: What is the difference between ArrayList and Vector?
options: Both are synchronized, but Vector is faster
ArrayList is synchronized while Vector is not
Vector grows by 50% while ArrayList doubles in size
Vector is synchronized (thread-safe but slower) and legacy; ArrayList is unsynchronized and faster. Vector doubles on resize, ArrayList grows by about 50%
questions.explanation: Prefer ArrayList; if you need thread safety use Collections.synchronizedList or CopyOnWriteArrayList rather than legacy Vector.

questions.question: What is the difference between HashMap and Hashtable?
options: HashMap is unsynchronized and allows one null key with many null values; Hashtable is synchronized and allows no nulls
Hashtable allows null keys while HashMap does not
Both are synchronized; Hashtable is simply the newer of the two
HashMap maintains insertion order while Hashtable sorts by key
questions.explanation: Hashtable is legacy. For concurrent access prefer ConcurrentHashMap, which locks at bucket level instead of the whole map.

questions.question: How does HashMap work internally?
options: It stores entries in a sorted binary search tree keyed by insertion order
It keeps a single linked list of all entries and scans it linearly
An array of buckets (default 16); hashCode() picks the bucket, collisions form a linked list that becomes a red-black tree past 8 entries (Java 8+), and equals() identifies the exact key
It hashes the value rather than the key and stores keys in a parallel array
questions.explanation: Bucket array sized to a power of two, hashCode for placement, equals for exact matching, and treeification of long collision chains since Java 8.

questions.question: What is the load factor of a HashMap?
options: The maximum number of entries a HashMap can ever hold
The fill threshold (default 0.75) at which the internal array doubles and entries are rehashed
The ratio of null keys to non-null keys
The number of buckets created at initialization, which defaults to 16
questions.explanation: At 75% occupancy the map resizes and rehashes. The value balances memory use against collision frequency.

questions.question: What happens when two keys produce the same hashCode?
options: The second entry silently replaces the first
The JVM throws a HashCollisionException
Both keys are rejected and put() returns null
A collision occurs — both land in the same bucket as a linked list (or red-black tree since Java 8), and equals() distinguishes them on lookup
questions.explanation: Equal hash codes do not mean equal keys. The bucket holds both entries and equals() resolves which one you asked for.

questions.question: What contract must hashCode() and equals() satisfy?
options: If a.equals(b) is true then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(); equal hash codes do not imply equality; and equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive and consistent
If two objects have the same hashCode they must be equal
hashCode() and equals() are independent and may safely contradict each other
Overriding equals() automatically overrides hashCode()
questions.explanation: Breaking this contract breaks every hash-based collection — objects get lost in HashMap and HashSet.

questions.question: What is the difference between HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap?
options: HashMap sorts by key, LinkedHashMap sorts by value, TreeMap keeps insertion order
HashMap has no order with O(1) average; LinkedHashMap preserves insertion (or access) order with O(1) average; TreeMap keeps keys sorted with O(log n) and disallows null keys
All three keep keys sorted and differ only in thread safety
TreeMap is O(1) while HashMap is O(log n)
questions.explanation: Pick HashMap for speed, LinkedHashMap when order matters (LRU caches use access order), TreeMap when you need sorted keys or range queries.

questions.question: What is the difference between HashSet and TreeSet?
options: HashSet is sorted while TreeSet is unordered
Both are backed by ArrayList internally
HashSet is unordered, O(1) average, backed by HashMap and allows one null; TreeSet is sorted, O(log n), backed by TreeMap and disallows null
TreeSet allows duplicates while HashSet does not
questions.explanation: TreeSet also implements NavigableSet, giving you first(), last(), headSet() and tailSet() for range operations.

questions.question: What is the difference between Iterator and ListIterator?
options: Iterator is forward-only and works on any Collection; ListIterator is bidirectional, works only on Lists, and supports add() and set() during iteration
ListIterator is forward-only while Iterator is bidirectional
Both can iterate over a Map directly
Iterator supports add() and set() while ListIterator does not
questions.explanation: ListIterator adds previous(), nextIndex(), add() and set() — but it is restricted to List implementations.

questions.question: What is the difference between fail-fast and fail-safe iterators?
options: Fail-safe iterators throw ConcurrentModificationException; fail-fast ones do not
Both iterate over a snapshot copy of the collection
Fail-fast iterators are only available on concurrent collections

Fail-fast throws ConcurrentModificationException if the collection is structurally modified during iteration (ArrayList, HashMap); fail-safe iterates over a copy without throwing but may miss recent changes (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap)
questions.explanation: Fail-fast uses a modCount check to detect concurrent structural modification. Fail-safe trades that safety for possibly stale data.

questions.question: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator?
options: Comparable uses compare() while Comparator uses compareTo()
Comparable defines the class's natural ordering via compareTo() inside the class (one order); Comparator is external via compare() and allows many different orderings
Comparator can only be used with TreeSet, never with sort()
Both must be implemented by the class being sorted
questions.explanation: Use Comparable when there is one obvious ordering you control; use Comparator (often as a lambda) for alternative or third-party-class orderings.

questions.question: How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety?
options: It locks the entire map on every read and write, like Hashtable
It makes a full copy of the map on every write
Java 7 used segment-level lock striping; Java 8+ uses CAS plus a synchronized lock on the first node of a bucket, giving far better concurrency than Hashtable's full-map lock
It is unsynchronized and relies on the caller for thread safety
questions.explanation: Fine-grained bucket-level locking means many threads can write to different buckets simultaneously — reads are usually lock-free.

questions.question: What is CopyOnWriteArrayList?
options: A thread-safe List where every write copies the underlying array — excellent for read-heavy, rarely-written data and poor when writes are frequent
A List that copies itself only when read, to protect the writer
A List that stores each element twice for fault tolerance
An unsynchronized List optimized for frequent insertions
questions.explanation: Reads need no locking at all since they see an immutable snapshot. Every add/set/remove allocates a fresh array, so writes are expensive.

questions.question: What is a BlockingQueue?
options: A queue that silently drops elements when it becomes full
A queue that blocks on put() when full and on take() when empty — the basis of producer-consumer designs (ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue)
A queue that can only be accessed by a single thread
A queue that orders elements by priority rather than arrival
questions.explanation: The blocking behaviour removes the need for manual wait/notify in producer-consumer code.

questions.question: What is a PriorityQueue?
options: A FIFO queue that ignores element ordering
A queue where the head is always the maximum element by default
A queue whose elements are ordered by natural ordering or a Comparator, with the head always the minimum element and O(log n) insert/remove
A thread-safe queue that blocks when empty
questions.explanation: PriorityQueue is a binary heap. Pass a reversed Comparator if you need a max-heap instead of the default min-heap.

questions.question: Can you store primitive types directly in Java collections?
options: Yes, collections store primitives directly for performance
Yes, but only int and double
No, and there is no workaround — you must use arrays
No — collections hold only objects, so primitives are autoboxed into their wrapper classes (int becomes Integer)
questions.explanation: Autoboxing happens automatically but costs memory and time, which is why primitive arrays or specialized libraries are used in hot paths.

questions.question: How do you make a collection read-only?
options: Use Collections.unmodifiableList/Map/Set(...), or since Java 9 the truly immutable List.of(...), Map.of(...) and Set.of(...)
Mark the collection variable as final
Declare the collection as static
Call the collection's lock() method
questions.explanation: final only stops reassignment of the reference, not mutation of the contents. unmodifiableXxx wraps a view; List.of() is genuinely immutable.

questions.question: What is an exception in Java?
options: A compile-time syntax error reported by javac
An abnormal event that disrupts normal program flow, represented as an object of Throwable or its subclasses
A warning the JVM logs but never acts on
A thread that has entered the BLOCKED state
questions.explanation: Exceptions are objects. Everything throwable descends from java.lang.Throwable.

questions.question: What is the exception hierarchy in Java?
options: Exception is the root, with Throwable and Error as its subclasses
Error and Exception are unrelated classes with no common parent
Throwable splits into Error (unrecoverable) and Exception (recoverable); Exception splits further into checked exceptions and unchecked RuntimeException subclasses
RuntimeException is the parent of both Error and Exception
questions.explanation: Throwable → Error (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) and Exception → checked plus RuntimeException (unchecked).

questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
options: Checked exceptions are verified at compile time and must be caught or declared (IOException, SQLException); unchecked ones extend RuntimeException and are not compiler-enforced (NullPointerException, ArithmeticException)
Checked exceptions occur at runtime while unchecked ones occur at compile time
Unchecked exceptions must be declared with throws while checked ones need not be
Both are enforced by the compiler and differ only in class hierarchy
questions.explanation: The compiler forces you to handle or declare checked exceptions. Unchecked ones usually signal programming bugs.

questions.question: What is the difference between throw and throws?
options: throw appears in the method signature while throws appears in the body
Both are used interchangeably in the method signature
throw catches an exception while throws rethrows it
throw actually throws an exception instance inside the body (throw new IOException()); throws declares in the method signature what the method may throw
questions.explanation: throw is an action taken on one exception object; throws is a declaration listing possible exception types.

questions.question: When does a finally block NOT execute?
options: finally never runs if the catch block executes
finally always runs after try/catch, except when the JVM exits via System.exit(), the thread is killed, or the try block loops forever or deadlocks
finally only runs when no exception is thrown
finally runs before the try block, to set up resources
questions.explanation: finally is for cleanup and runs on both the success and exception paths — only JVM termination or a non-returning thread prevents it.

questions.question: Can you have a try block without a catch block?
options: Yes — try-finally is valid, and try-with-resources needs no explicit catch either
No, every try must have at least one catch
Yes, but only inside a static method
Yes, but the class will not compile without a throws clause
questions.explanation: A try needs either a catch or a finally (or to be a try-with-resources). It cannot stand completely alone.

questions.question: What is try-with-resources?
options: A block that retries the try body if an exception occurs
A way to allocate more heap memory to a try block
A Java 7+ syntax that automatically closes any resource implementing AutoCloseable, removing the need for a manual finally block
A construct that catches all exceptions silently
questions.explanation: Resources declared in the try(...) header are closed automatically in reverse order, even if an exception is thrown.

questions.question: Can you catch multiple exception types in one catch block?
options: No, each exception type needs its own catch block
Yes, since Java 7: catch (IOException | SQLException e) — and the caught variable is implicitly final
Yes, using catch (IOException && SQLException e)
Yes, but only if the exceptions share a direct parent class
questions.explanation: Multi-catch uses the pipe symbol and removes duplicated handling code. The types must not be in a subclass relationship with each other.

questions.question: Can a finally block override a return statement in try?
options: Yes — a return inside finally overrides the one in try, though it is considered bad practice and static analyzers warn about it
No, the try block's return always wins
No, a finally block cannot contain a return statement
Yes, but only for void methods
questions.explanation: It also silently swallows exceptions thrown in try, which is exactly why linters flag returning from finally.

questions.question: How do you create a custom exception in Java?
options: Implement the Throwable interface and override throw()
Annotate a class with @Exception and give it a message field
Extend Error and override getMessage()
Extend Exception for a checked exception or RuntimeException for an unchecked one, adding constructors that delegate to super
questions.explanation: Choose the parent based on whether callers should be forced to handle it. Give it a meaningful name like InsufficientBalanceException.

questions.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
options: A thread has its own memory space while a process shares memory with other processes
A process is an independent program with its own memory space; a thread is a lightweight unit of execution inside a process, sharing the heap but with its own stack
Threads and processes are the same thing in Java
A process is created by calling start() and a thread by calling run()
questions.explanation: Threads share the heap (hence the need for synchronization) but each gets its own stack and program counter.

questions.question: How do you create a thread in Java?
options: Only by extending Thread and overriding start()
By implementing Callable and overriding run()
Either extend Thread and override run(), or implement Runnable and pass it to a Thread — the second is preferred since it leaves inheritance free and works with lambdas and executors
By annotating a method with @Thread
questions.explanation: Runnable is preferred: Java allows only one superclass, and Runnable is a functional interface so it works as a lambda and with ExecutorService.

questions.question: What is the difference between start() and run()?
options: start() creates a new thread and invokes run() on it; calling run() directly just executes the code on the current thread with no concurrency
run() creates a new thread while start() only prepares it
Both create a new thread; start() is simply the newer API
start() can be called repeatedly on the same Thread object
questions.explanation: Calling run() directly is a classic bug — the code executes sequentially on the caller's thread. Calling start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException.

questions.question: What are the thread states in Java?
options: CREATED, OPEN, CLOSED, DESTROYED
READY, RUNNING, SUSPENDED, STOPPED
INIT, ACTIVE, PASSIVE, DEAD
NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED
questions.explanation: These are the values of the Thread.State enum. Note that Java does not distinguish RUNNING from RUNNABLE at the API level.

questions.question: What does the synchronized keyword do?
options: It guarantees a variable's value is always read from main memory
It locks an instance (synchronized method), a class (synchronized static method) or an object (synchronized block) so only one thread executes the protected section at a time
It creates a new thread for the marked method
It makes a method run without ever being interrupted by the scheduler
questions.explanation: synchronized provides both mutual exclusion and visibility. Locking the smallest useful scope (a block) beats locking a whole method.

questions.question: What does the volatile keyword guarantee?
options: It makes compound operations like count++ atomic
It prevents a field from ever being modified
It guarantees visibility — a write by one thread is immediately visible to others and the value is not cached in registers — but it does NOT guarantee atomicity
It is simply a synonym for synchronized applied to a field
questions.explanation: volatile solves visibility, not atomicity. For atomic compound updates use AtomicInteger or synchronization.

questions.question: What is the difference between wait(), sleep(), and yield()?
options: wait() releases the lock and waits on an object's monitor inside a synchronized block; sleep() pauses the thread for a set time without releasing locks; yield() is only a hint to the scheduler
All three release any locks the thread currently holds
sleep() releases the lock while wait() does not
wait() and sleep() are both static methods on Thread
questions.explanation: The key exam point: wait() releases the monitor, sleep() does not. wait() is called on an object; sleep() and yield() on Thread.

questions.question: What is a deadlock?
options: A thread that runs forever without producing output
A thread that is never scheduled because higher-priority threads dominate the CPU
An exception thrown when two threads write the same variable
Two or more threads waiting forever for locks held by each other in a cycle — prevented by fixed lock ordering, tryLock timeouts, and avoiding nested locks
questions.explanation: Deadlock requires a circular wait. Acquiring locks in a consistent global order is the simplest practical prevention.

questions.question: What is the difference between a race condition, livelock, and starvation?
options: All three are different names for the same deadlock condition

Race condition: unsynchronized access to shared state gives unpredictable results. Livelock: threads keep running and reacting to each other but make no progress. Starvation: a thread never gets resources because others monopolize them
Livelock means the threads are blocked while deadlock means they are running
Starvation only occurs in single-threaded programs
questions.explanation: Deadlock = blocked forever. Livelock = busy forever with no progress. Starvation = runnable but never scheduled.

questions.question: What is the Executor / ExecutorService framework?
options: A class that forces every task to run on the main thread
A JVM subsystem that schedules garbage collection
A Java 5 abstraction for thread management — instead of creating threads manually you submit tasks to a reusable thread pool such as Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)
A replacement for the synchronized keyword
questions.explanation: Thread pools cap the number of live threads and reuse them, avoiding the cost and unpredictability of unbounded manual thread creation.

questions.question: What is the difference between Runnable and Callable?
options: Runnable.run() returns void and cannot throw checked exceptions; Callable<V>.call() returns a value and can throw checked exceptions, and pairs with Future
Callable returns void while Runnable returns a value
Both return values, but only Runnable works with executors
Callable can only be used with a single thread
questions.explanation: Use Callable whenever the task produces a result or may fail with a checked exception — submit() gives you a Future for the outcome.

questions.question: What is the difference between Future and CompletableFuture?
options: Both are blocking and functionally identical
Future is a placeholder for an async result with a blocking get(); CompletableFuture (Java 8) is non-blocking and composable via thenApply, thenCompose and thenCombine with async callbacks
CompletableFuture always blocks the calling thread until completion
Future was introduced in Java 8 to replace CompletableFuture
questions.explanation: CompletableFuture lets you build a pipeline of dependent async steps without ever blocking a thread on get().

questions.question: What is the Java Memory Model (JMM)?
options: The layout of the heap into young and old generations
The set of rules the JIT compiler uses to inline methods
The algorithm the garbage collector uses to reclaim objects
The specification of how threads interact through memory — which writes are visible to which reads, the semantics of volatile, synchronized and final, and the happens-before relationship
questions.explanation: The JMM is what makes concurrent Java reasoning possible: happens-before defines exactly when one thread's write is guaranteed visible to another.

questions.question: What is the difference between CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier?
options: CountDownLatch is one-shot — threads wait until a count reaches zero and it cannot be reused; CyclicBarrier makes threads wait until all parties arrive and is reusable after tripping
CountDownLatch is reusable while CyclicBarrier is one-shot
Both are reusable and differ only in naming
CyclicBarrier counts down from a fixed number while CountDownLatch waits for all parties
questions.explanation: Latch: wait for N events to complete, once. Barrier: N threads meet at a rendezvous point, repeatedly.

questions.question: What are atomic classes such as AtomicInteger?
options: Wrapper classes that make primitives immutable
Classes that internally use a synchronized block on every method
Lock-free thread-safe classes in java.util.concurrent.atomic that use CAS (Compare-And-Swap) for atomic updates without synchronization overhead
Classes that guarantee visibility but not atomicity, exactly like volatile fields
questions.explanation: CAS retries in a loop until the update succeeds, avoiding lock contention. incrementAndGet() is atomic where a volatile int++ is not.

questions.question: Which set of features was introduced in Java 8?
options: Records, sealed classes, pattern matching and text blocks
Lambda expressions, Stream API, functional interfaces, method references, default/static interface methods, Optional and the java.time API
Generics, annotations, autoboxing and the enhanced for loop
Modules, the var keyword and the new HTTP client
questions.explanation: Java 8 was the functional-programming release. Generics/annotations came in Java 5; modules in 9; records and sealed classes in 14-17.

questions.question: What is a lambda expression?
options: A named method that can be called without an object
A special type of anonymous class that must extend Thread
A concise anonymous function you can pass around like data, written as (params) -> expression, assignable only to a functional interface
A compiler directive that enables parallel execution
questions.explanation: A lambda is an inline implementation of a functional interface's single abstract method — far less ceremony than an anonymous class.

questions.question: What is a functional interface?
options: An interface with exactly one abstract method (default and static methods do not count) — such as Runnable, Comparator, Predicate or Function — optionally marked @FunctionalInterface
An interface that contains only static methods
An interface that must be implemented by at least one lambda
Any interface annotated with @Override
questions.explanation: The single abstract method is what a lambda binds to. @FunctionalInterface makes the compiler enforce the rule.

questions.question: What is the Stream API?
options: A replacement for InputStream and OutputStream in java.io
A data structure that stores elements in sorted order
A thread pool used to process collections in parallel
An abstraction for processing sequences of elements declaratively — filter, map, reduce, collect — that is lazy, consumes a source, and supports parallel execution
questions.explanation: Streams describe what to compute rather than how to loop. They do not store data and can only be consumed once.

questions.question: What is the difference between intermediate and terminal stream operations?
options: Intermediate operations trigger execution while terminal ones are lazy
Intermediate operations return a new stream and are lazy (filter, map, sorted, distinct); terminal operations trigger execution and produce a result (collect, forEach, reduce, count)
Both are eager and execute immediately when called
Terminal operations can be chained indefinitely while intermediate ones cannot
questions.explanation: Nothing runs until a terminal operation is invoked — which is why a stream pipeline with no terminal call does nothing at all.

questions.question: What is the difference between map() and flatMap()?
options: map() flattens nested streams while flatMap() performs a one-to-one transform
Both perform identical transformations and differ only in return type
map() applies a function to each element as a one-to-one transform; flatMap() applies a function returning a stream and then flattens the results into a single stream
flatMap() can only be used on primitive streams
questions.explanation: Use flatMap when each element expands into many — for example turning a List<List<String>> into a single stream of Strings.

questions.question: What is Optional in Java 8?
options: A container for a possibly-absent value that forces explicit handling via isPresent(), orElse(), map() and ifPresent() — intended for return values, not fields or parameters
An annotation that marks a method parameter as not required
A collection that can hold at most two elements
A wrapper that automatically replaces null with a default of zero
questions.explanation: Optional makes absence part of the type signature, pushing callers to handle it instead of hitting a NullPointerException.

questions.question: What is a method reference?
options: A pointer to the memory address of a method, as in C
A way to call a method before its class is loaded
A reflection API call used to invoke private methods
Shorthand for a lambda that only calls an existing method — String::toUpperCase instead of s -> s.toUpperCase() — in static, bound instance, unbound instance and constructor forms
questions.explanation: Method references are pure syntax sugar over lambdas, and they read better when the lambda body is a single existing call.

questions.question: What are default methods in interfaces?
options: Methods called automatically when no other method matches
Methods with a body inside an interface (Java 8+) marked with default, which let new methods be added to an interface without breaking existing implementations — how List.forEach was introduced
Methods the compiler generates for every interface automatically
Private helper methods that only the interface itself can call
questions.explanation: Default methods solved interface evolution: the Java team could add forEach and stream() to Collection without breaking every existing implementation.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Collection and a Stream?
options: Both store data in memory and can be reused indefinitely
A Stream stores the data while a Collection processes it
A Collection stores data in memory, while a Stream is a computation pipeline that processes data without storing it — lazy, single-use and parallelizable
A Stream is simply a synchronized Collection
questions.explanation: Collections are about efficient storage and access; streams are about expressing a computation over that data.

questions.question: What is serialization in Java?
options: Converting an object into a byte stream for storage or transmission (deserialization reverses it) — the class must implement Serializable, transient skips fields, and serialVersionUID handles version compatibility
Converting a byte stream into a running thread
Compressing an object so it occupies less heap space
Making all of an object's methods synchronized
questions.explanation: Serializable is a marker interface with no methods. Mark sensitive or derived fields transient so they are not written out.

questions.question: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?
options: A shallow copy duplicates nested objects while a deep copy shares them
A shallow copy copies fields as-is so nested object references are shared; a deep copy recursively duplicates nested objects, producing a fully independent object
Both produce fully independent copies and differ only in performance
A deep copy is produced automatically by Object.clone()
questions.explanation: Object.clone() gives a shallow copy by default — mutating a nested object through either reference affects both copies.

questions.question: What are generics and type erasure?
options: Generics are enforced at runtime by the JVM using reified types
Type erasure converts List into List<String> when the class is loaded
Generics exist only for documentation and have no compile-time effect
Generics give compile-time type safety (List<String>), and type erasure strips that information at runtime (List<String> becomes List) for backward compatibility with pre-generics code
questions.explanation: Because of erasure you cannot do new T[] or instanceof List<String> at runtime — the type argument simply is not there anymore.

questions.question: What is garbage collection, and can you force it?
options: Yes — System.gc() immediately and reliably runs a full collection
No, Java has no garbage collector; memory is freed with free()
GC automatically reclaims unreachable objects; System.gc() only suggests a collection and the JVM decides — algorithms include Serial, Parallel, G1 (default since Java 9), ZGC and Shenandoah
GC runs only when the heap is completely full and cannot be influenced at all
questions.explanation: System.gc() is a hint, not a command. Objects become eligible for collection when they are no longer reachable from any GC root.

questions.question: How do ==, equals(), and hashCode() differ for objects?
options: == checks reference identity, equals() checks logical equality, and hashCode() returns an int used by hash-based collections — if you override equals you must override hashCode consistently
All three compare object contents in exactly the same way
hashCode() compares two objects and returns a boolean
Overriding hashCode() automatically provides a correct equals()
questions.explanation: Override both together for value-based classes, otherwise HashMap and HashSet will fail to find objects you just inserted.
